chunks: Aban, from Abdullah ibn Sulayman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
What the snare seizes, so something is cut off from it, or it dies, then it is dead meat (mayta).

key_terms.الْحِبَالَةُ: The snare or trap (hibala) — a hunting device that catches animals by entanglement, as opposed to projectile weapons
key_terms.مَيْتَةٌ: Mayta — dead meat/carrion; legally impermissible flesh of an animal that died without proper Islamic slaughter

ai.seo_question: Is an animal caught in a trap considered halal or haram to eat in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issues a ruling on animals caught in snares or traps: if the trap severs a limb from the animal, or if the animal dies in the trap, then that animal (or severed part) is classified as mayta — dead meat that is religiously impermissible (haram) to consume. This ruling distinguishes trap-caught animals from those properly slaughtered (dhabh), as Islamic law requires ritual slaughter with the invocation of God's name. The original audience of jurists would have understood mayta as a specific legal category encompassing all animals that die without proper Islamic slaughter.

en.hubeali:
Aban, from Abdullah Bin Suleyman, 
Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> has said:
‘What the snare seizes, so something is cut off from it, or it dies, so it is dead’.
en.sarwar: 4. Aban has narrated from ‘Abd Allah ibn Sulayman who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘
Whatever of the prey is caught in the snare which is cut off or has died is dead.’”
